title: Turn the hearts (Malachi 4:5–6)
hook: the last lines of the Protestant Old Testament: hearts of parents turned to children

segments.voice: Yesterday, your king comes on a donkey, lowly and riding, with no warhorse. Your line was lowly, riding. Where did you choose the donkey instead of the horse? Day four hundred ninety-six.

Open most Protestant Bibles to the end of the Old Testament, and turn one more page. On the left, the last verse of Malachi. On the right, usually a blank page, and then the first line of Matthew, a list of names. That blank page stands for roughly four centuries. So whatever Malachi says last is the final word before the long wait. You might expect a grand vision, or a thunderclap. Instead, the final words are about something very small and very close to home. They're about families. Parents and children. Who's speaking to whom, and who isn't.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE, THEN A BLANK ONE.`

segments.voice: Malachi's name means my messenger, and it may be a title rather than a name. His book is a series of arguments between God and the people, about tired worship, broken promises and marriages, and the poor being cheated. Then the end, in the King James Bible: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers." Elijah, remember, never died in the old stories. He was carried up in a whirlwind. So the hope grew that he'd come back, to prepare the way for God. Jews still set a place for Elijah at the Passover table and open the door for him. And look at what Elijah's work will be. Not to defeat enemies. To mend families. To turn hearts across the generations, in both directions. Parents toward children, and children toward parents. Then the very last words warn that otherwise God will strike the land with a curse. That ending is so hard that in synagogue readings the verse before it is read again afterward, so the book closes on Elijah and hope. You'll hear these words again very soon. In the opening chapter of Luke, an angel promises that a child named John will come in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Christians read John the Baptist as the Elijah Malachi promised. So the Old Testament, in this arrangement, ends with a family reunion still waiting to happen.
screen: then, large: `HE SHALL TURN THE HEART OF THE FATHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call a parent or child. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone a generation away from you: a parent or a child, or if they're gone or far away, a grandparent, a niece, a mentor, someone you've cared for. Picture their face. Notice what's between you: warmth, distance, an old hurt, a thing unsaid. Don't try to fix it all. Just let your heart turn toward them, a few degrees, the way Malachi pictures it. Then decide on one small contact: a call, a message, a photo, a visit. If you pray, you can bring them before God by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Turn the hearts. Malachi's last promise: Elijah will come and turn the hearts of parents to children, and children to parents.
Your line: turn the hearts. Today, make the call or send the message you chose. Ask one question and actually listen to the answer. Day four hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Christians often read Malachi in Advent, as the prophecy of a messenger before the Lord, and many churches pair it with the Gospel stories of John the Baptist.

myth: every Bible ends the Old Testament with Malachi
most Protestant Bibles do. the Jewish Bible ends with Chronicles, and other Bibles order the books differently.
Malachi promises Elijah will turn hearts in both directions
parents toward children, and children toward parents.
Jews still set a place for Elijah at Passover
many families set a cup for him and open the door during the meal.

fork.setup: Elijah is coming back before the great day of the LORD. what does Malachi say his work will be?
options: turning the hearts of parents and children toward each other.
fork.reveal: not battles but families: "he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers."

original.note: Hebrew: my messenger. it may be a title for the prophet rather than his name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Old Testament just stops.
what it means: its last word in many Bibles is a promise that Elijah will come and mend families across the generations.
what a scholar hears: in synagogue readings the verse before the curse is read again, so the book ends on Elijah, and Luke 1 applies the promise to John.

sources.quoted: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD: And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers

notes: Malachi 4:5–6 are 3:23–24 in Hebrew Bibles. In synagogue reading, 3:23 is repeated after 3:24 so as not to end on a curse; confirm.
'Roughly four centuries' between Malachi (c. 5th century BC) and the New Testament era; approximate and common. Confirm phrasing.
Whether 'Malachi' is a name or title ('my messenger', cf. 3:1) is debated; presented as 'may be'.

Canon order: Protestant OT ends with Malachi; Hebrew Bible ends with 2 Chronicles; Douay-Rheims and some Catholic/Orthodox Bibles place Maccabees or other books differently. Stated neutrally; confirm.
Elijah's cup and opening the door at the seder: a neighbor's practice, mentioned without comparison.
